How the game works

Fifty-five marbles, twenty-eight moves

Marbles sit on a hexagonal board of 91 cells. You clear them in matching pairs, and you win by clearing the lot. Two rules do all the work.

A marble is only free if three of its six neighbours are empty and touching

Not any three — three in a row around it. Two gaps on opposite sides do not count. Space off the edge of the board counts as empty, which is why the rim clears first and the middle is the fight.

What matches what

  • The four elements — fire, water, earth, air — pair with their own kind.
  • Salt pairs with any element, or with another salt. It is the flexible one, and only four exist.
  • Vitae and mors pair only with each other.
  • The five metals go in order of transmutation — lead, tin, iron, copper, silver — each with a quicksilver. Tin cannot go while lead is still down.
  • Gold clears alone, once it is the last metal standing.

A full deal is always the same multiset: eight of each element, four salt, four vitae, four mors, five quicksilver, and one of each metal. That adds up to 55 marbles and exactly 28 moves — 27 pairs and the gold. The count turns out to matter enormously later.

Solving it

A search that fits in one integer

A marble never moves, so its position tells you its type. That means the whole state of a game is just which cells are still occupied — 91 bits, one integer. The solver is a depth-first search over those integers that remembers every state it has proven unwinnable, so a dead end reached by a different order of moves is recognised instead of re-explored.

Freedom is a lookup, not a calculation. Each cell's six neighbours are stored in cyclic order, so "three contiguous empty spaces" is a window over a 64-entry table. Directions that run off the board point at a bit that is never set, so edge cells count their missing sides as empty for free.

Two facts about the game shape the search

Removing marbles never blocks anything. Freedom only ever increases. So the difficulty is not the order of the moves, it is the pairing: spend a salt on an element that still had a partner of its own kind, and you can orphan a marble twenty moves later. Salt is therefore played last, and the search carries a parity check — each element left in an odd number must consume a salt, and the leftover salt has to pair with itself. Positions failing that are dead before the search notices.

Metals are forced. Only the lowest metal on the board can go, and only against quicksilver, so those moves have no alternative pairing and cost nothing to take early.

Restarts, and why the jitter has to be big

Solving times are heavy-tailed. The median board falls in 29 states; every so often one choice near the root buries the search in a barren subtree. So the search runs in rounds of doubling budgets, re-shuffling its tie-breaks each round, and keeps the set of dead states across rounds — deadness does not depend on how a state was reached, so a restart never repeats prior work, it only re-picks its gambles.

The size of the shuffle turned out to be the whole trick. With a small jitter, restarts only reshuffled marbles within a class of move, kept re-walking the same doomed opening, and the two worst boards in 300 needed over 1.5 million states. Making the jitter large enough to reconsider which kind of move to open with brought both under 140,000.

Two good ideas that measurement threw out

  • Scoring moves by how many marbles they actually unlock searched fewer states but cost more wall-clock than it saved.
  • A fixpoint "could this marble ever be freed?" prune never fired once across 600 boards — these boards die on pairing, not geometry — and cost two to three times as much.

Test boards are built backwards — pairs of a solution placed onto an empty board in reverse, each required to land free — so every generated board comes with a guaranteed solution, and the solver is checked against a real oracle rather than its own output.

Reading the board off a screenshot

Finding a hexagon, then fifty-five glyphs

Transcribing 55 marbles by hand is miserable, so the next step was to read them from a picture. Two problems: find the board, then name every cell.

Finding it

The playing surface is far brighter than the metal around it, so a brightness split isolates it — chosen per image, because a fixed threshold read the reference perfectly and then lost 60 cells on a copy 20% brighter. The board is a hexagon whose extent in a few directions pins down its centre and scale.

On a whole desktop the board is not the biggest bright thing — a bright wallpaper beats it easily — so candidates are ranked by shape rather than size. A board's width and height imply the same cell size and it fills the area that size predicts; the wallpaper scored 37% skew and 0.55 fill against the board's 3% and 1.06.

Naming the cells

The game draws blocked marbles washed out and free ones vivid, so the features have to ignore that entirely. Each cell is high-pass filtered — the tile minus a blurred copy of itself — which throws away the marble's shading and the cell's bevel and leaves the engraved glyph, then normalised so faint and bold match. Colour enters only as a direction: the disc's colour minus the cell background, scaled to unit length, because fading a marble toward the beige changes that vector's length but not its heading.

Three things were found by measuring rather than assuming:

  • Plain contrast-stretched brightness gets 96.5% of cells, and its mistakes are exactly fire↔earth and vitae↔salt — pairs the eye separates instantly. The marble's radial shading dominates the tile and the glyph is a small part of the signal. High-pass filtering takes it to 100%.
  • "Empty" has to be a template class, not a brightness threshold. Six blocked marbles — faint vitae, salt, quicksilver — sit below the brightest empty cell, so no threshold separates them. Their glyphs are unmistakable.
  • Templates are stored at several small offsets each. Detection lands within a pixel or two but not exactly, and matching a glyph against a template shifted 2px loses the outer ring of cells.

The reader refuses rather than guessing when the board is too small to resolve, cut off by the crop, or not a board. Whatever slips past that is caught by the marble counts, because a misread almost always shows up as some count differing from a standard deal.

The constraint that fixed the last bug

A long automated run once died after one win: lead read as mors — both dark marbles, and lead has the fewest examples because it appears once per board. The fix was to stop reading a fresh deal cell by cell. The counts are known exactly, so the board is solved as an assignment against them: the cell that has to be the lead is the one that fits it least badly.

Testing that fix caught something worse. Imposing the counts always succeeds — on a board still animating in, it cheerfully invented 55 marbles from an empty table, and because the counts then matched by construction, the check that was supposed to validate the deal had been destroyed. A visible bug had been replaced with a silent one. So the constrained result is only accepted when the plain read already saw a full board and needed at most a couple of cells overruled.

Playing the real game

Screenshot, solve, click, verify

The last piece drives the actual game: screenshot the monitor, find the board among everything else on screen, read it, solve it, and click the pairs. It talks to Windows directly rather than through an automation library, because the usual one scales its coordinates by the display's DPI setting and so misses every click on a 4K screen.

It checks its own work

The loop is deliberately not "solve once, then fire 56 clicks and hope". After every pair it re-reads those two cells and confirms they actually went empty. A click that misses leaves the plan and the board disagreeing, and every later click then lands on the wrong marble — so it retries, more slowly, and then gives up on that board rather than clicking on blind.

Failures say which thing went wrong, because the fixes differ: "they read as Fire and Water, which do not match — misread" versus "the pair still matches, so the click did not register". It also watches the game's own wins counter after each board. It never reads the number, only sees the box change, which is enough to confirm the game agreed — and that caught a real bug immediately, when a board left already-cleared from an earlier run "solved in 0 moves" and was scored as a win while the counter sat still.

Making it quick

The first version took 1.37 seconds a move, nearly 40 seconds a board. Almost none of it was the clicking:

  • Screen capture cost 110ms a go, whatever the size. The imaging library rebuilds its device contexts on every call, so grabbing forty pixels cost the same as grabbing a 4K screen. Holding them open across calls takes the same grab to 6ms, pixel for pixel identical.
  • Verifying a move re-read all 91 cells to look at two. Reading just those two costs 27ms against 370.
  • A fixed 450ms sleep waited for the clearing animation. Polling instead finishes as soon as the pair actually goes.

That is 227ms a move, about six seconds a board. What is left is the game's own animations: dealing takes 4.3 seconds and nothing can hurry it, so the loop waits by watching the board stop changing — an idle board measures a frame-to-frame difference of exactly zero, which makes "still" unambiguous. It waits for the animation to start first, because the deal does not begin until 400ms after the click and the board is otherwise trivially still the moment it is asked.

What is running where

On this page, and in the repository

Everything above this line runs in your browser — the rules, the search, and the screenshot reader are ported from the Python, using the same templates cut from two real screenshots. The solver here matches the original state for state: the reference board solves in 83.

The Python project adds what a browser cannot do: driving the real game. It ships a command line tool, a local web front end for checking the rules by hand, and the autoplay loop, with 113 tests covering the geometry, every matching rule, the search, the reader and the click layer. The autoplay tests stub out the screen and the mouse entirely — nothing in the suite moves a real pointer.

Built with Claude Code against Opus Magnum by Zachtronics. The puzzle, its artwork and its alchemical glyphs are theirs; this is a solver for it.
